newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian election campaign swings into high gear.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian election campaign swings into high gear.

text.p: Indonesian politicians campaigned from the far west of Sumatra to the jungles of Irian Jaya on Monday as the fight for nearly 125 million votes in May 29 general elections swung into high gear.

There were no reports of trouble in the world's fourth most populous nation of 200 million people after a smooth start to the campaign on Sunday and financial markets rebounded strongly after a pre-campaign attack of nerves last week.

The only trouble reported in the capital were scuffles with police involving supporters of defendants from the Marxist-leaning People's Democratic Party (PRD) on trial in Jakarta. The party is banned from taking part in the election,
Only three parties are legally permitted to run for the 425 elected seats in the House of Representatives. The other 75 seats are alloted to the military which does not vote.

The Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), badly split since its leader Megawati Sukarnoputri was ousted by government-backed rebels last year, produced a low-key campaign on the main island of Java and in the remote Muluks and Irian Jaya.
Its leader Surjadi was in Jakarta, but party officials said they were unable to provide a schedule -- "We operate on a day-to-day basis," one official said.
The PDI won 15 percent of the vote in the last elections in 1992.

The ruling Golkar, seeking to push its share of votes above the 70 percent mark after winning 68 percent in 1992, campaigned on the government's development policies in Sumatra, the resort island of Bali and the adjacent Nusa Tenggara islands.

The Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP), which accused the state broadcaster of pro-Golkar bias, campaigned in Kalimantan on Borneo island and Sulawesi in a bid to boost its take from the 17 percent won in 1992.
Financial markets rebounded as the campaign got under way after fears last week of possible violence.

The rupiah, which tumbled 15 points at one point last week, rose sharply to 2,426 to the dollar from an opening of 2,436 and dealers said the currency remained in favour on sound economic fundamentals.
The stock market composite index also rose just over four points to 656.5, mainly on buying by local speculators with foreign investors largely remaining on the sidelines.
A Reuters poll of securities analysts saw an average rise in the index of 2.3 percent by the end of June and 12.25 percent by the turn of the year.

Juwono Sudarsono, professor of politics at the University of Indonesia, said the campaign's calm start could be attributed to some extent to former PDI chief Megawati's appeal to her supporters to exercise restraint and keep out of the campaign.
"It seems it augurs well for the moment," Sudarsono added.
Brokers expected thin volume and possible volatility on the stock market, but anticipated a surge in post-election prices.

"We think that volume will continue to be thin, which leads to some volatility, and that the market will be pretty directionless up to the elections," Felix D'Sousa, head of research at PT Peregrine Sewu Securities, told Reuters.

"But we think that after the elections, the focus will swing back to the very well managed, steady economy, and people will see very strong corporate earnings growth coming through. I think the market will perform very strongly," he said.
